_comment: Permission safety rails shipped by workbench-core and merged into
~/.claude/settings.json by scripts/permissions.sh (additively — an entry is
only ever added, never removed).
Rules are evaluated deny → ask → allow, before the auto-mode classifier, in
every permission mode including bypassPermissions. That is the point: a
boundary stated only in conversation is lost when context is compacted, but
a deny rule is not.
HEADLESS CONSTRAINT — read before adding to `ask`:
An ask rule always forces a prompt, and a `claude -p` run has nobody to
prompt, so the call is blocked instead. workbench-dev-team dispatches Watson
unattended via `nohup claude -p --agent`, and Watson pushes branches, commits,
and opens PRs. So `Bash(git push:*)`, `Bash(git commit:*)`, and
`Bash(gh pr create:*)` are deliberately NOT in `ask` — putting them there
would kill the pipeline silently. The git-commit approval gate stays a
PreToolUse hook, which can carry a pipeline exemption; an ask rule cannot.
LINUX COVERAGE — why there is no pacman/apt/dnf rule:
`Bash(sudo:*)` is denied, and every mutating system-package operation needs
root, so those managers are already walled. Only the ROOTLESS paths needed
new rails: AUR helpers (run as your user, elevate internally), `systemctl
--user`, `systemd-run --user`, polkit-mediated `udisksctl`, and libsecret.
A blanket pacman rule would prompt on every harmless `-Q` query for no gain.
DATABASE DENIES — why they are here AND in a hook:
This file guarded disks, git history, and `rm`, and said nothing about
databases. On 2026-09-04 `php artisan db:wipe --database=pgsql --force` ran
with no prompt, because no rule matched, and dropped every table in a
development database. The deny rules below are the declarative layer — the
boundary a human can read in /config. They are NOT the enforcement.
A deny rule matches a command PREFIX, and the incident shape was
`cd /repo && php artisan db:wipe`, where the verb is not at the front. The
same command also reaches a database through `sail`, `docker compose exec`,
`ssh host "..."`, and `bash -c "..."`, and raw `DROP DATABASE` arrives as
the payload of `psql -c` or a heredoc — none of which a prefix can express.
hooks/destructive-database-guard.sh tokenises the command and reads the verb
SLOT, so it covers every one of those. Keep both: the rule is visible, the
hook is enforcing.
WHY THERE IS NO `php artisan` DENY RULE — do not add one:
The four reset verbs (db:wipe, migrate:fresh, migrate:reset,
migrate:refresh) are guarded by the hook ALONE, on purpose. The incident was
a wrong TARGET, not a wrong verb: rebuilding the testing database is ordinary
work, so the hook allows a reset that scopes itself with --env=testing or
--database=testing. A deny rule cannot carry that exemption, because a prefix
cannot read a flag that comes later. Add `Bash(php artisan migrate:fresh:*)`
here and the exemption dies silently: the hook exits 0, which is neutral
rather than an allow, and the deny rule blocks the call anyway.
That mistake would also be sticky. scripts/permissions.sh merges this file
into ~/.claude/settings.json additively and never removes an entry, so
deleting the rule here later does not take it back out of a user's settings.
dropdb, dropuser, and mysqladmin drop have no such exemption — there is no
legitimate agent use — so those DO ship as denies below.
The same split governs Docker. `docker volume rm` and `docker volume prune`
ship as denies: they delete volumes outright, and a containerised database
keeps its data in one. `docker compose down` does NOT, and must not — the
plain form leaves named volumes alone and is how a stack is routinely
stopped. Only `down --volumes` destroys data, and that flag sits AFTER the
subcommand where a prefix cannot read it. The hook handles that case, along
with `docker rm -v`, `docker system prune --volumes`, and `sail down -v`.
`lando destroy` and `wp-env destroy` ship as denies for the same reason —
one verb, no legitimate agent use, nothing to read past it. `ddev delete`
does NOT, and that is deliberate: `ddev delete images` removes Docker
images rather than project data, and a prefix rule would block it too. The
hook makes that distinction. This is the third instance of the same rule,
so state it plainly — a deny rule belongs here only when the FIRST WORDS of
the command decide the outcome. Whenever the verdict depends on a flag or a
later argument, the hook is the enforcement and a deny rule is a trap.
The disk-tool denies are defense in depth on the same footing as `dd` and
`mkfs` — they need root too, but the deny costs nothing and does not depend
on the sudo rule staying in place.
WHY THERE IS NO Read() DENY RULE — do not add one back:
This file used to ship four: Read(~/.ssh/**), Read(~/.aws/**),
Read(~/.gnupg/**), and Read(**/.env). They cost far more than they gave.
1. They were never enforcement. Anthropic's permissions documentation is
explicit that Read and Edit deny rules apply to the built-in file tools and
to the file commands Claude Code recognises in Bash — cat, head, tail, sed —
and NOT to arbitrary subprocesses that read files indirectly, like a Python
or Node script that opens a file itself. OS-level enforcement across every
process is the sandbox, not a deny rule.
2. Any one of them armed a large permission-prompt class. In the Claude Code
binary (v2.1.259, function `duo`, circuit breaker `deniedPathInsideDirectory`)
`xce()` is a plain boolean over alwaysDenyRules: if ANY Read() deny rule
exists, then for grep/egrep/fgrep/rg/diff/git/cp/mv a non-absolute path
argument in a command containing `cd` returns behavior "ask" without ever
consulting a rule — the prompt reading "after a cd would search a directory
that cannot be determined here, and a Read() deny rule is configured". The
breaker is registered bypassImmune with no classifier route, so auto mode
never sees it and no allow rule overrides it. Narrowing the rules does
nothing; only removing every Read() rule disarms it.
The replacement is hooks/credential-guard.sh, a PreToolUse hook that exits 2
before permission rules are evaluated. It covers strictly more than the deny
rules did: it catches `python3 -c "print(open('~/.ssh/id_rsa').read())"`,
which a Read deny never touched. hooks/test-permissions.sh asserts that no
Read() rule creeps back in.

deny.why: Nothing the agent does should need root.
Raw block-device writes destroy disks with no undo.
macOS disk format/erase/partition.
Linux partition table editing. macOS consolidates this under diskutil; Linux spreads it across several binaries, so each needs its own rule.
Partition table editing. `cfdisk` and `gdisk` are deliberately absent — they are interactive TUIs, so a non-interactive shell hangs on them rather than silently destroying a table.
Scriptable partition table editing — the non-interactive fdisk, and so the one an agent could actually drive to completion.
Scriptable GPT editing. Same reasoning as sfdisk.
Erases filesystem signatures, leaving a volume unmountable with no undo.
Discards every block on a device. Unrecoverable.
Irreversible overwrite. Denied rather than asked: unlike `rm`, which is legitimate constantly, an agent has no routine reason to securely wipe a file.

`btrfs subvolume delete` destroys snapshots, which on a btrfs root are the undo rope for every other mistake — the same reasoning as the reflog rule below. Arch-derived systems including Omarchy root on btrfs by default.
Filesystem creation over an existing volume. Prefix matching means this also covers the per-filesystem variants — `mkfs.ext4`, `mkfs.btrfs`, `mkfs.vfat`.
Irreversible and outward-facing.
Rewrites remote history. Prefix matching means this also blocks `--force-with-lease` — accepted tradeoff.
Bulk history rewriting.
Destroys the reflog, which is the undo rope for every other git mistake.
Bulk credential dump. Scoped find/add/delete are handled by ask rules instead, since plugin setup skills use them.
Destroys a PostgreSQL database outright. No undo, no prompt.
Destroys a PostgreSQL role, taking its owned objects' access with it.
Deletes a named volume, which is where a containerised database keeps its data. `docker volume ls` and `docker volume inspect` are unaffected — the rule is scoped to the verb.
Deletes every unused volume at once, including a stopped database's. There is no per-volume confirmation and no undo.
Destroys a lando app and the database it owns. Scoped to the verb, so `lando start`, `lando rebuild`, and the rest are untouched.
Destroys the wp-env environment and its WordPress database. Same verb scoping as the lando rule.

Destroys a MySQL database outright. Scoped to the verb rather than blanket, because `mysqladmin status` and `mysqladmin ping` are ordinary health checks. The flag form `mysqladmin -u root drop app` slips past this prefix, and is caught by the hook instead — which is the whole argument for having both layers.

ask.why: The only rm guard, by design. A deny on `rm -rf /` would match every absolute-path delete (prefix matching, and `*` is always a wildcard), and cannot carry a /tmp exception since deny beats allow regardless of specificity. Claude Code already handles root and home removals semantically: the classifier decides them in auto mode — including inside $(...) and <(...) substitution — and they still prompt in bypassPermissions as a circuit breaker. So prompt here and let the built-in breaker cover the catastrophic case.
Discards uncommitted work.
Deletes untracked files, including ones never staged.
Discards stashed work.
Discards every stash at once.
Human merge is already the pipeline's gate — make it enforced, not conventional.
Outward-facing and hard to retract. No dev-team agent does this unattended.
Publishing to a public registry is effectively permanent.
Removes system tooling other work depends on.

AUR helper — the Linux package-manager gap the `sudo` deny does NOT close. pacman/apt/dnf need root for every mutating operation and are already walled by that deny; an AUR helper runs as your user and elevates internally, so it slips past. Blanket rather than scoped to `-R`, because the install path builds and executes arbitrary PKGBUILD code as your user, which is the more dangerous half. Accepted cost: read-only queries prompt too.
The other common AUR helper. Same reasoning as yay.
Installs or removes background persistence.

The launchctl analogue — installs or removes background persistence, and `--user` needs no root. Blanket rather than scoped to enable/disable/mask, because the flag precedes the verb: `Bash(systemctl enable:*)` would not match `systemctl --user enable foo`, which is precisely the rootless case most in need of the rail.
Creates transient units, and `--user` needs no root.
Mounts, unmounts, and powers off block devices through polkit — without sudo.
Installs or removes scheduled persistence.
Keychain write. Plugin setup skills use this, and those run interactively, so a prompt is fine.
Keychain deletion.

libsecret write — the Linux keychain analogue. Scoping to the verb is reliable here, unlike systemctl, because secret-tool always takes its verb as the first argument. That leaves `lookup` unprompted, mirroring `security find-generic-password` on macOS.
libsecret deletion.

_autoMode_comment: `autoMode.allow` entries are prose exceptions to the classifier's built-in
soft-deny rules — a different layer from permissions.deny/ask, which are tool
patterns evaluated BEFORE the classifier runs.
DANGER: the literal string "$defaults" must appear in the array. Without it,
Claude Code replaces the entire built-in soft-deny list — force push,
`curl | bash`, production deploys, auto-mode bypass, all of it. permissions.sh
The classifier reads autoMode only from ~/.claude/settings.json and managed
settings — never from .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json, so a repo

allow.rule: Dispatching workbench-dev-team agents is allowed: the scheduled Dispatch task launches `nohup claude -p --agent workbench-dev-team:<lestrade|watson|holmes> --dangerously-skip-permissions` as a detached subprocess. This is the sanctioned pipeline entry point, not Claude removing its own oversight — each dispatched agent runs under its own guardrails, work is scoped to one board item, and every result lands in a human-reviewed pull request.
allow.why: The classifier's built-in soft-deny list includes auto-mode bypass, and this command is Claude spawning itself with --dangerously-skip-permissions — which reads exactly like an oversight bypass. A soft deny clears on explicit user intent, but a scheduled task has no user message to clear it, so dispatch is blocked non-deterministically. Confirmed live 2026-07-22 (x2), 2026-07-25 (Holmes and Watson both denied), still open 2026-07-29. This entry is the documented fix: an exception to a soft deny is precisely what autoMode.allow is for. A permissions.allow rule is the wrong lever — auto mode deliberately suspends broad shell allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution.
